analysis.one_liner: Lets states permanently waive EPA air-pollution rules on power plants by claiming reliability or affordability.
analysis.headline: The bill to let states permanently waive EPA power-plant pollution rules died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let any state governor, by certifying that power plants are needed to keep electricity reliable and affordable, permanently opt the state out of any EPA air-pollution rule for electric generating units. In practice, that could exempt coal- and gas-fired power plants from Clean Air Act limits. The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Power-plant owners — especially operators of coal- and gas-fired generating units — would gain the most, since a governor's certification would permanently lift EPA air-pollution rules on their plants, avoiding compliance costs. State governors would also gain sweeping new power over federal environmental regulation within their borders. Ratepayers might see some savings on electricity bills in states that use the waiver, though that depends on how much compliance costs actually feed into rates.

how_it_helps.text: State governors could permanently waive any EPA regulation on electric generating units, by certifying the plants are needed for power reliability and affordability.
Because the waiver applies to any Clean Air Act regulation on power plants, it could override rules limiting pollution from coal- and gas-fired plants.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost through increased air pollution from power plants, with health effects concentrated in communities near generating units. People who live downwind would also share the burden, since pollution crosses state lines.

drawbacks.text: A governor's certification is the only requirement — no hearing, no review of whether the power plants really are needed for reliability, and no check on the claim, so the waiver could be used to escape clean-air limits entirely.
The waiver is permanent, so once a state opted out, EPA could not enforce those pollution rules on its power plants again under the waiver.
Reduced air-pollution enforcement on power plants would shift health costs — asthma, heart disease, smog — onto the public, while the savings accrue to plant operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is hard to see and falls on everyone: permanent EPA waivers could let power plants avoid air-pollution limits for decades, with health and environmental damage concentrated near plants. The benefit side is real but indirect — potentially cheaper electricity in states that use the waiver — and largely depends on what the rules being waived actually required. As drafted, the bill gives one official unchecked authority to set aside federal pollution rules permanently, with no independent verification, which is a poor trade for public health.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate environment committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe of Oklahoma introduced the bill on February 4, 2014.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing EPA power-plant rules stayed in force, so the public kept current clean-air protections; the bill's absence preserved the regulatory status quo rather than delivering new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA's existing power-plant rules survived untouched

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: Coal and electric utility interests
for.what_they_did: Generally opposed EPA power-plant regulation during this period, the constituency the bill was designed to serve.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support on record.

industries.note: The bill would let states permanently waive EPA air-pollution rules on power plants, cutting compliance costs for plant operators. Utilities, especially coal-heavy ones, would be the direct beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and cleaner power generators
industries.note: Weaker pollution rules on fossil plants would remove a cost disadvantage their competitors would otherwise face, making it harder for cleaner sources to compete.
